pages.title: Non-small-cell lung cancer
pages.subtitle: Physician discussion packet
blocks: Selected evidence for a surgical consultation. Educational sample; independent clinical review pending.

Dear Dr. ____________________,
I would like your assessment of whether the repurposing studies in this packet are relevant to my diagnosis and proposed treatment. Please help me understand the strongest evidence, the important limitations, and whether a clinical trial or specialist second opinion would be appropriate within the treatment timeline you recommend.

If an approach is unsuitable, I would appreciate a specific explanation of whether the issue is evidence quality, a mismatch with my cancer or treatment setting, safety, or another concern. Please help me record the reasoning and agreed next steps on the final page.
Surgery can be curative for selected patients with resectable NSCLC, and treatment depends on disease stage, histology and the patient's health.{{1}}

The four selected reports do not establish that itraconazole or metformin can replace potentially curative surgery. The presurgical itraconazole study retained planned surgery; the other trials evaluated additional drugs in different treatment settings.{{2,3,4,5}}

pages.title: Itraconazole studies
pages.subtitle: Exploratory clinical findings and their limits
blocks: Gerber and colleagues enrolled 13 patients with NSCLC scheduled for resection. They received itraconazole for 10-14 days before surgery, with imaging, blood and tissue measurements to investigate biological effects.{{2}}

Higher drug concentrations were associated with greater reductions in tumor volume and perfusion, among other measurements. These short-term associations do not establish improved survival or show that surgery can safely be omitted.{{2}}
Question for the physician: Does this type of presurgical research have any relevance to my case, and is an appropriate trial available without disrupting the planned treatment schedule?
Source basis: published abstract reproduced in the authors' institutional publication record. This is a biological-effects study, not a comparison of itraconazole against surgery.
With chemotherapy after prior metastatic treatment

Rudin and colleagues conducted an open-label randomized phase 2 trial in previously treated metastatic nonsquamous NSCLC. It enrolled 23 patients: 15 received pemetrexed plus itraconazole and 8 received pemetrexed alone. The trial closed early because of slow recruitment as pemetrexed use changed.{{3}}

At 3 months, 67% versus 29% were progression-free (P = .11), the primary endpoint. Median overall survival, an additional endpoint, was 32 versus 8 months (P = .012), favoring the combination. The authors emphasized that the small sample made effect estimates highly unstable.{{3}}

Reported events in the combination group included transient grade 4 neutropenia without fever and a possibly treatment-related intratumoral bleed within 30 days after leaving the study. This small study cannot establish broad safety or a reliable survival benefit, and it did not study initial treatment of resectable disease.{{3}}
Question for the physician: Does this trial match my treatment history and histology, and what corroborating evidence would be needed before its findings could influence my care?
The U.S. capsule label warns about heart failure, serious liver toxicity and consequential drug interactions, including contraindicated combinations involving CYP3A4 substrates.{{6}}

Ask the oncology team and pharmacist to review the complete medication list, relevant heart and liver history, and any proposed monitoring. A drug's established use for another illness does not by itself establish its suitability for this cancer treatment.
These two studies address different questions. Their findings are not combined into a treatment recommendation or a single benefit estimate.

pages.title: Metformin studies
pages.subtitle: Randomized trials with no benefit or concerning outcomes
blocks: This open-label phase 2 trial studied patients without diabetes who had unresectable stage III NSCLC. Of 170 enrolled patients, 167 eligible patients were analyzed: 86 in the metformin group and 81 in the control group. Both groups received chemoradiation and consolidation chemotherapy.{{4}}

The primary endpoint, 1-year progression-free survival, was 51.3% with metformin and 60.4% without it (hazard ratio 1.15; 95% CI 0.77-1.73; P = .24). One-year overall survival was similar, and no significant difference in adverse events was reported. The trial did not demonstrate improved survival with metformin.{{4}}
Discussion implication: This trial provides no demonstrated benefit for adding metformin to the tested regimen in this population. It does not compare metformin with surgery.
Source basis: PubMed abstract. Full methods, protocol and supplement appraisal remain incomplete for this sample.

This open-label phase 2 trial randomized 54 patients without diabetes and with unresected stage III NSCLC: 26 to chemoradiotherapy plus metformin and 28 to chemoradiotherapy alone. Recruitment stopped early.{{5}}

The primary composite treatment-failure endpoint occurred within 1 year in 18/26 patients (69.2%) with metformin versus 12/28 (42.9%) in the control group (P = .05). It included progression, death, or stopping trial treatment or planned evaluations for any reason.{{5}}

One-year overall survival was 47.4% versus 85.2% (hazard ratio 3.80; 95% CI 1.49-9.73). At least one grade 3 or higher adverse event was reported in 14/26 (53.8%) versus 7/28 (25.0%), respectively. These are all-cause adverse events, not all established as caused by metformin.{{5}}
The small sample, open-label design and treatment imbalances limit interpretation; the unfavorable findings argue against an anticancer add-on in this setting.{{5}}

Ask: If I already use metformin for diabetes, how should that indication and my treatment plan be managed? These trials studied an anticancer add-on in people without diabetes. Do not change an existing diabetes prescription because of this packet.

The studies on these two evidence pages used different populations, treatment combinations and outcomes. Side-by-side results cannot establish which drug is superior or predict an individual patient's outcome.

PFS means progression-free survival. OS means overall survival. A hazard ratio describes relative event rates over follow-up; it is not a percentage-point change in survival. CI means confidence interval.

pages.title: Sources and scope
pages.subtitle: Original reports and clinical context
blocks: The numbered links below open original source records. Research summaries distinguish the tested setting and reported result from the discussion implications. No formal evidence-certainty grade or individualized treatment recommendation has been assigned.

This is a selected-source discussion sample featuring four reports published in 2013, 2020 and 2021. Sources were checked on October 12, 2026. It is not a systematic review, a complete list of repurposing candidates, or a comprehensive search of research through that date.

Summaries of Gerber 2020 and NRG-LU001 use accessible abstracts. Rudin 2013 and OCOG-ALMERA use accessible full-text sections. Complete study appraisals and independent clinical review are pending. Patient details are intentionally blank; applicability must be established with the care team.
Prepared as an AI-assisted RemapRx product sample. This edition has not been approved for clinical or commercial distribution. Article PDFs are not reproduced; use the source links for access.

pages.title: Discussion and next steps
pages.subtitle: Patient and physician worksheet
blocks: Use this page to capture the explanation and agreed actions. A decision to continue the current plan can be a useful outcome when its reasons are clear.
What is the treatment goal, why is this plan recommended, and what timing matters?
Assess the relevance of the research
Which study, if any, fits my stage, histology, biomarker results and treatment history?
If a repurposed approach is unsuitable, what is the reason and what evidence could change that assessment?
Are any tests, a thoracic oncology opinion, tumor board review or a trial inquiry appropriate? Can these happen within the recommended treatment timeline?

"To make sure I have understood: we are recommending ____________________ because ____________________. The next step is ____________________, and we will revisit this if ____________________. Is that accurate?"
Before sharing a completed copy, confirm the recipient and use the practice's preferred patient portal or secure communication method.
